extracted.intended_audience: lovers of poetry, literary critics, and the educated public interested in evaluating or promoting poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and selecting poetry (with a focus on Wordsworth) emphasizing subject-matter, poetic truth, style, inspiration, and the social/moral purpose of poetry and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deals with life
rubrics_metrics.description: The best and master poets 'deal with life' — i.e., with that in which life really consists. Great poetry treats the real substance of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is what distinguishes great poets; English poets are praised for dealing 'with what is really life.' Example: Wordsworth's greatness lies in dealing with life as a whole, more powerfully than many other celebrated poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful dealing with life (completeness/wholeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's superiority may be judged by how much of 'life as a whole' he deals with and how powerfully he does so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth is commended for dealing with 'more of life' and 'life as a whole' more powerfully than Burns, Keats, Heine, etc. Preference given to poets who render broad, comprehensive human experience rather than only isolated moods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs. philosophical abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry must possess 'poetic' truth; mere philosophical or abstract statements, even if elevated, lack the character of poetic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: passages that are 'a tissue of elevated but abstract verbiage, alien to the very nature of poetry' (example: many lines in the Excursion). When philosophy takes on the 'form and habit of a scientific system of thought' in poetry, it often becomes illusion rather than the reality that poetry should be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical material must become poetic
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet treats philosophical ideas, those ideas must be transformed into genuine poetic expression rather than remaining formal or didactic systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworthians who praise the poet for his formal philosophy misunderstand his strength; the poetry (not the systematic philosophy) is the reality to be valued. Example of failure: doctrinal passages rendered as abstract proposition rather than poetic insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and accessibility of subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet takes from sources of joy and experience that are 'accessible universally' — matters in 'widest commonalty spread.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage: telling of what all seek and from its truest and best source; the source should be one where 'all may go and draw.' This gives poetry broad appeal and moral weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination in selection and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everything a great poet writes is equally excellent; critics and advocates must discriminate among a poet's works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Wordsworthians praising all works indiscriminately (e.g., equating 'The Sailor's Mother' with 'Lucy Gray'). The critic should select and present the poems that best serve the public's appreciation of the poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration and inevitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry at its best should feel inspired and 'inevitable' — as if Nature herself wrote it; when inspiration is absent, poetry is left weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth's poetry is sometimes 'inevitable' and glorious when inspiration is upon him; when inspiration fails he is 'left weak as is a breaking wave.' Aim for spontaneous, inevitability-bearing expression rather than contrived lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assured poetic style (heightening by style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic style — an assured, characteristic manner — gives subtle heightening and elevation to verse; it is an essential component of poetic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of assured style: Shakespeare, Milton. Wordsworth lacks a consistently assured poetic style but occasionally attains lines of such quality. When a poet 'has a style' it raises and refines even comparatively modest imaginative material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness, sincerity, and first-hand naturalness
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain, direct, sincere manner can be a virtue when it relies on the weight and force of true feeling and faithful representation of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Burns' plainness influenced Wordsworth; poems like 'Resolution and Independence' are 'bald' yet grand. Plainness should be genuine and suited to the subject, not a mask for poverty of imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of truth of subject and truth of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The best poems perfectly exhibit a balance between profound truth of subject and profound truth of execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion of excellence: both what is told (subject matter) and how it is rendered (craft, execution) must be true and powerful. Examples recommended to show this balance: 'Michael', 'The Fountain', 'The Highland Reaper'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of ponderosity, pomposity, and forced style
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet seeks artificially to impose style or system, the result tends toward ponderosity and pomposity; genuine poetry resists such contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: the _Excursion_ as a stylistic product that can fall into ponderous manner; when Wordsworth 'seeks to have a style he falls into ponderosity and pomposity.' Value spontaneous naturalness over affected grandiloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive simplicity (highest kind of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy and simplicity in phrasing can achieve the highest expressiveness (e.g., 'And never lifted up a single stone').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine expressive simplicity is not a lack of craft but a refined choice. Such lines show that subtle heightening can be achieved without ornate diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotive rendering: make the reader share the joy or feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should 'show us' joy or feeling and 'render it so as to make us share it' — i.e., evoke empathy and participatory feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that make the reader partake of the poet's experience rather than merely describe it; this is part of what makes Wordsworth powerful when he succeeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive solidity of poetic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic generalizations (e.g., about childhood instincts) should have substantive solidity and not rest on doubtful universal assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Wordsworth's 'intimations' about childhood instincts are beautiful as fancy but lack 'real solidity' as universal claims. Critics should be wary of sweeping psychological generalizations presented as poetic doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and social efficacy of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ideally 'will cooperate with the benign tendencies in human nature and society' and be 'efficacious in making men wiser, better, and happier.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative standard: part of poetry's value is its capacity to improve human character and society, not merely to please or astonish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as the study of perfection (sweetness and light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture should be understood as the study and pursuit of perfection — a harmonious inward condition combining 'sweetness and light' (beauty and intelligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine culture from superficial smattering; culture's motive is not mere exclusiveness but the desire to augment the excellence of our nature and to 'make reason and the will of God prevail.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture combines scientific passion and moral/social passion
rubrics_metrics.description: True culture joins the scientific passion ('desire to see things as they are') with the social/moral passion ('love of our neighbor' and desire to do good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture should not be solely intellectual curiosity nor solely activist zeal; both rigorous thought and beneficent impulse are necessary to reach harmonious perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection as inward, general, and harmonious expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection (the goal of culture) is an inward condition: the harmonious expansion of all powers, general across humanity, not the over-development of any single faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultural products (including literature) by whether they cultivate inward character, balance faculties, and promote general human betterment rather than merely external or mechanical advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to worship of machinery, wealth, or mere material greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound cultural/literary standard resists treating machinery (railroads, coal), wealth, population, or bodily vigour as ends in themselves; these are means, not measures of greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spiritual and aesthetic standards (culture's standards) to judge works and societies; culture should 'purge' the mind of philistinism and materialistic vulgarity and help set true standards of perfection.
